traps.why: HIO₄ is an oxidative cleavage: each carbinol carbon ends up at the carbonyl level. If you drew alcohols, no oxidation happened and the C–C bond would still be intact.
The CH–OH carbon had one carbon neighbour and one H, so it becomes an aldehyde, not a methyl ketone. Only the carbon that carried the CH₃ becomes a ketone.
That is what PCC would do to the 2° alcohol. HIO₄ does not oxidise an alcohol in place; it cleaves the C–C bond between the two OH-bearing carbons.
Periodate cleavage stops at the aldehyde. Going on to the carboxylic acid is Jones/chromic acid chemistry, not HIO₄.

nameTraps.name: heptane-2,6-dione
nameTraps.why: Carbon 1 has only one carbon neighbour, so it is an aldehyde (-al), not a second ketone.

nameTraps.name: 2-oxoheptanal
nameTraps.why: The aldehyde carbon is always C1, so the ketone sits on C6, not C2.

explanation: HIO₄ breaks the C1–C2 bond of the diol. C1 (bearing CH₃) has two carbon substituents → ketone; C2 (bearing H) has one → aldehyde. The ring opens into a single seven-carbon chain: 6-oxoheptanal.
tip: Cut between the two OHs, then count carbons on each cut end: two C's → -one, one C → -al.

traps.why: HIO₄ cleaves the C2–C3 bond; it does not oxidise the alcohols in place to a diketone.
Periodate cleavage stops at the aldehyde. Acids would need chromic acid.
Cleavage is oxidative: each carbinol carbon becomes a carbonyl, not an alcohol.

nameTraps.name: ethanone
nameTraps.why: A two-carbon carbonyl with an H on the carbonyl carbon is an aldehyde: ethanal.

explanation: The C2–C3 bond is cleaved; each CH(OH)CH₃ becomes CH₃CHO. Two molecules of acetaldehyde.

traps.why: HIO₄ stops at the aldehyde.
The carbinol carbons are oxidised to carbonyls as the bond breaks; alcohols would mean no oxidation happened.
Benzil would keep the C–C bond; HIO₄ breaks it.

explanation: Cleavage between the two carbinol carbons gives two benzaldehydes.
tip: Each half keeps its aryl group and gains a C=O.

traps.why: Cleavage oxidises both ends to aldehydes; a diol would mean the C–C bond broke without oxidation, which never happens.
HIO₄ stops at the aldehydes.
A diketone keeps the ring; HIO₄ opens it.

nameTraps.name: pentanedione
nameTraps.why: Both ends are CH=O: aldehydes, so -dial.

nameTraps.name: 1,5-pentanedial
nameTraps.why: Aldehyde locants are always 1 (and the last carbon), so they are dropped: pentanedial.

explanation: The ring opens at the C1–C2 bond; both carbons had one H, so both become aldehydes: pentanedial.
tip: Cyclic diol → one chain with a carbonyl at each end.

traps.why: The aldehyde is not oxidised further by HIO₄.
Each cut end is oxidised to a carbonyl, not left as an alcohol.
That is PCC chemistry (oxidising the 2° OH in place). HIO₄ breaks the C2–C3 bond.

explanation: C2 (two methyls) becomes acetone; C3 (ethyl + H) becomes propanal.
tip: Two carbons on the cut carbon → ketone; one carbon → aldehyde.

traps.why: Both cut ends become carbonyls, not alcohols.
HIO₄ stops at the aldehydes.
A diketone keeps the C–C bond; HIO₄ breaks it.

explanation: The C1–C2 bond breaks: C1 (phenyl + H) becomes benzaldehyde, C2 (methyl + H) becomes acetaldehyde.
tip: Each cut carbon keeps its own substituents and gains a C=O.

traps.why: Each cut end is oxidised to a ketone.
That is the pinacol rearrangement (hot H₂SO₄, no periodate). HIO₄ cleaves instead.
Any vicinal diol reacts with HIO₄, 3° carbinols included.

nameTraps.name: propanal
nameTraps.why: The carbonyl carbon carries two methyls and no H: a ketone, propan-2-one.

explanation: Both carbinol carbons carry two methyls, so cleavage gives two molecules of acetone.
